idiom_name: class per table (fields = columns) + finder object or static finders + insert/update/delete on the instance
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one class per table whose fields mirror the columns, put the find operations either in static methods or in a separate finder class per table, and give every instance insert/update/delete plus a load step that fills the fields from a result row. Clients hold the business logic and the transaction scope; the gateway holds only data access. Decide explicitly where row identity is managed - without an identity map two finds produce two objects and the later update wins - and generate the classes from metadata once more than a handful of tables exist.
code_sketch:
class PersonGateway:                 # one class per table
    fields: id, last_name, first_name, deps     # one field per column

    @staticmethod find(connection, id) -> PersonGateway   # SELECT ... WHERE id = ?
    @staticmethod find_responsibles(connection) -> [PersonGateway]

    def insert(connection)   # INSERT INTO people ...
    def update(connection)   # UPDATE people SET ... WHERE id = ?
    def delete(connection)   # DELETE FROM people WHERE id = ?
pitfalls: Letting domain logic creep into the gateway: the moment the class decides business rules it has become an Active Record and the separation the pattern buys is gone.
Forgetting that finders and updates must run inside the caller's transaction; a gateway that opens its own connection cannot join the script's unit of work.
Looping over finders per row instead of writing one set-based statement.

Wrong move: Put discounts, validation or workflow rules on the gateway -> it becomes an Active Record and couples persistence to domain policy -> instead keep those rules in the transaction script or service.
Wrong move: Call find once per item in a loop -> row-at-a-time gateways create N+1 round trips and allocations -> instead issue one set-based query or a batch finder for the collection.

Wrong move: Let each gateway open or commit its own connection -> callers cannot compose several row writes into one atomic unit of work -> instead inject and reuse the caller's connection and transaction.
